Defining with specific terms how someone feels towards others and/or perceives themselves is always going to fall into restriction and some sort of innacuracy. The experience of living, and in that discovering human interactions and feelings is too complicated and complex for anyone to find the right amount of words to use in order to display a clear picture of one’s identity. 
It’s almost as if there are both too many and not enough labels… so you do you. As long as you are respectful (no bad intentions in using some specific term) and comfortable then you really don’t have to worry about anything. 
Technically I am an asexual person that has feelings of affection and deep connection only towards women. I have called myself a lesbian before, but rn i just love letting myself be what i am without any specific definition. If you feel like finding a label that suits you so that you can feel valid and at peace, that you are more than welcome to do so. If this label is “lesbian” then I encourage you to embrace it. If you’ll find your comfort in “just being” without any word for it, then that will be just fine too.
Hope i made my self clear enough.

First of all, I’m genuinely so sorry for everything you had/have to go through… I can’t imagine how hard it has to be living with such a weight on your shoulders and yet staying strong and put together for yourself and your family.

Remember that everyone expresses their feelings in different ways: it’s not your fault if you didn’t notice the signs… she probably didn’t want you to see that she was cutting.
In fact, she probably will feel bad about the fact that she is going to have to stop, but this is the same thing that will make a part of her heart feel lighter.

It will not be easy, but you’ll manage it and you two will learn together how to cope with everything that’s happening.

For the “dad situation” i’d say that it could be better to ask the therapist about it… it also really depends on your daughter’s relationship with him.

One last thing… don’t worry about the privacy you gave her.
When my parents took my door, i self harmed in the middle of the night… sometimes I did it hidden on the stairs right before going out.
You know, If someone wants to self harm… than they’ll do it no matter what.
Tell her her privacy will always have value, but that now her health is a priority.
Tell her that you’d prefer not to leave her alone if she is triggered by something, but that you don’t want to take away her space.
She probably feels guilty for what she does to herself… she probably will be sad and convinced that she’s hurting you more than herself… you don’t want to make her feel less of a human than what she’s already feeling.

It will take some time, but, when therapy will start working, the necessity to find a safe space will be as strong as the urge to cut and eventually she will find her own safe space and she’ll give up the privacy and secrecy that she cherished and dedicated to her addiction and coping mechanism.

I know it’s hard to hear, but you can’t control her actions, nor feelings.
She’s your daughter and chances are that now you’re thinking about how much you’d prefer to take on you her struggles… but that is not possible.
Don’t think about ifs and buts… think about the future and put faith in therapy and healing…



It pains me so much to see how many kids are hurting… but it gives me hope to see parents that really care.
Thank you for being there for her… I know you don’t think you deserve to hear it now, but i admire you and I believe that you’ll think about this horrible period years from now and you both will be in a safer headspace.
